stops.name: Magdala: the castle of Magdalo, her lineage
stops.campa: Mary is born of a lineage the Golden Legend calls royal: her father Cyrus, her mother Eucharis, landholders of Galilee and Judea. The inheritance divides three ways among the children: Lazarus takes the portion in Jerusalem, Martha the estate at Bethany, and Mary the fishing town on the western shore of the lake, the castle of Magdalo, whence she is called Magdalene. She grows up rich, fair, and, the tradition does not soften it, given over to the pleasures her wealth affords her, in the town that will one day carry only her own name.

stops.name: Magdala, the seven devils cast out
stops.campa: Luke names her plainly among the women who follow the Teacher: Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils. The Gospel gives no more than the fact and lets the number stand for whatever completeness of ruin a soul can hold: seven, the number of the whole. Jesus speaks, and the multitude of spirits goes out of her at once, not one by one. She does not return to the pleasures of Magdala. She turns instead and follows the man who emptied her, and gives what she owns to the work of his kingdom.

stops.name: Cana of Galilee, witness to the first sign
stops.campa: Among the guests at the wedding in Cana, where the wine fails and the stone jars of water are filled to the brim at Mary the mother's word, the newly healed woman of Magdala stands with the small company that has begun to gather around the Teacher. She watches the servants draw out wine where there had been only well-water, watches the astonishment of the governor of the feast. It is the first sign, and she is present at it, one of the company who will follow this abundance all the way to the far end of loss and back again.

stops.name: Capernaum: the sinful woman's tears, a tradition folded into her
stops.campa: At the house of a Pharisee, the Gospel does not name the town; the West's long tradition sets the scene here in Capernaum, where a woman known through the city as a sinner comes in uninvited, weeping, and stands behind him at the table. She washes his feet with her tears, dries them with her unbound hair, and anoints them from an alabaster box, while the Pharisee looks on in scorn. He tells her that her sins are forgiven, for she loved much. Centuries of the Latin church will fold this woman into Magdalene herself, though the Gospel never gives her a name.

stops.name: The Sea of Galilee: Joanna, Susanna, and the provisioning of the Twelve
stops.campa: Luke sets her name beside two others seldom heard again, Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza, and Susanna, and says only that these, and many more, minister to him of their own substance. It is the plainest sentence in the Gospel and the largest one: a company of women, some of means, fund the Teacher's traveling household out of their own purses, cook, carry, and keep the Twelve fed on the road between towns. Mary of Magdala, once emptied of seven devils, becomes one of the hands that keeps the kingdom's business running while the men are sent out to preach it.

stops.name: Mount of Beatitudes, hearing the Sermon
stops.campa: On the green hill above the lake she sits among the crowd that has followed him up from the shore and hears the new law given: blessed are the poor, the mourning, the meek, the merciful, the persecuted. She who was cast out of herself by seven devils and given back whole hears the promise made first to those the world discards. Whatever she carries away from the mountain that day, she will carry it all the way to a grotto in another country, thirty years from now, where meekness and mourning become the whole of her daily bread.

stops.name: Nain, witnessing the raising of the widow's son
stops.campa: At the gate of Nain a dead man is carried out on a bier, the only son of a widow, and Jesus stops the funeral with a single word: Young man, arise. Among the women who witness it, tradition places Mary of Magdala, watching a mother's mourning turned in an instant into a mother's son restored. She has already been given back her own life once, emptied of what possessed her; now she watches him give a whole widowed house its life back too, and understands a little more of what following this man will mean, and what it will someday cost her.

stops.name: Bethany: the raising of Lazarus, her brother
stops.campa: Lazarus lies four days in the tomb, and his sister goes out to meet the Teacher on the road before he even reaches the house: Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. It is the same sentence Martha has already spoken, word for word, and the Western church will read both sisters as one woman under two names: Mary of Bethany folded into Mary of Magdala. Whichever telling is followed, she stands at the tomb mouth when the stone is rolled back and hears the four-days-dead man called out of the dark by his own name.
stops.quote: Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.

stops.name: Jericho: on the road up, Bartimaeus and Zacchaeus
stops.campa: On the road up out of Jericho, in the press that surrounds blind Bartimaeus crying for mercy and gathers beneath the sycamore where the tax-man Zacchaeus has climbed to see him, Mary of Magdala walks among the company going up to Jerusalem for the last time. She has followed this road for four years now, Galilee to Judea and back, provisioning, watching, learning what the kingdom costs its own. Ahead lies the city, the Passover, and the single week the Gospels will remember longer than almost any other week in the whole history of the world.

stops.name: Bethany, the anointing at Simon's house
stops.campa: Six days before the Passover, at supper in the house of Simon, Mary takes a pound of costly spikenard and anoints the Teacher's feet, wiping them with her unbound hair until the whole house is filled with the fragrance. Judas objects that it might have fed the poor; Jesus answers that she has kept this against the day of his burying, and that wherever the Gospel is preached this deed will be told for a memorial of her. Whether this Mary is the sister of Lazarus or the woman once healed at Magdala, the tradition does not fully untangle the two, and does not need to.

stops.name: Golgotha, standing at the cross
stops.campa: Many of the disciples have fled; the women do not. Mark names her first among those who stand and watch from a distance while the cross is lifted: Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome. She has followed him from Galilee, ministering to him with her own hands, and she does not leave now that ministry can no longer help him: only watch, through the three hours of darkness, through the cry of dereliction, through the last breath and the tearing of the Temple veil, to an end that is not, though no one there yet knows it, the end.

stops.name: The Tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, the burial watched
stops.campa: Joseph of Arimathea takes the body down at evening, and Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit over against the sepulchre and watch where he is laid: the Gospel's own word, beholding, as if seeing itself were now the only service left to give. She marks the rock, the garden, the great stone rolled to the door, because she means to come back the moment the Sabbath allows it, with spices, to do for the body what Friday's haste did not allow. She is the last to leave the tomb that night, and, though she cannot know it yet, will be the first to return to it.
